summary: Reviewed all 16 in-scope files in full and checked relevant call paths. Four P1 issues exist: the unauthenticated dashboard exposes PII to other local users, generic submissions can trust attacker-controlled registry URLs, DNS failures can bypass the generic URL guard, and confirmation clicks can be reported as successful without evidence.

findings.title: Default loopback dashboard has no authentication
findings.what: When no auth file or credentials are configured, every request passes authentication. The default server binds to loopback, which other local accounts on a shared host can also access; `/api/config` returns the user's personal fields.
findings.trigger: Start the dashboard with no AIDR credentials or auth file on a shared NAS or VPS, then have another local account request `/api/config`.
findings.impact: Another local user can read the user's identity data and access other dashboard endpoints, including those that start real runs.
findings.fix: Require authentication for sensitive dashboard routes even on loopback, or provide a mode that explicitly restricts access to the owning user.

findings.title: Registry URLs can direct PII to an unrelated public site
findings.what: Feed rows are accepted as broker URLs based on an `http` prefix, without checking that the host belongs to the named broker. The generic runner can then fill and submit an opt-out-looking form on that site.
findings.trigger: A poisoned or compromised registry row supplies an attacker-controlled public URL with an opt-out path and form.
findings.impact: The unattended run can submit the user's name, email, address, and other configured fields to the attacker's site.
findings.fix: Require an operator-approved broker host or a verified domain match before automating a feed entry.

findings.title: DNS lookup errors fail open and cached verdicts can permit SSRF
findings.what: A failed or timed-out DNS lookup is treated as allowed. `makeUrlChecker` then caches that positive verdict by origin, while Playwright resolves the host independently, so the browser can reach a private address without the landing check detecting it.
findings.trigger: A registry URL uses an attacker-controlled host whose DNS lookup times out or returns a public IP to Node, then resolves to a private address for the browser.
findings.impact: The browser can send requests to internal services; if the returned page has a fillable opt-out form, the runner may also send the user's PII there.
findings.fix: Fail closed on DNS errors and validate or pin the destination IP for the browser's actual requests and redirects.

findings.title: Any non-rejected 2xx confirmation page is recorded as success
findings.what: After checking only the HTTP status and a short list of rejection phrases, `clickConfirmLink` returns `ok: true` without requiring positive confirmation evidence. The caller then records success.
findings.trigger: A confirmation link returns HTTP 200 or 204 with a login wall, generic page, or other response that contains none of the rejected phrases.
findings.impact: The pending request is marked confirmed and skipped for 90 days even though the broker may not have completed the opt-out.
findings.fix: Require a positive confirmation signal; treat unknown response pages as unverified and keep the request pending.

findings.title: Editing an encrypted config writes it to plaintext first
findings.what: On an already-encrypted install, setup writes the updated full config to `config.json` before re-encrypting and shredding it later. An interruption or encryption failure leaves that plaintext file behind.
findings.trigger: Rerun setup with a readable encrypted config and the process stops or encryption fails after `saveConfig(config)`.
findings.impact: The config, including PII and credentials, remains unencrypted on disk; an in-place encrypted config may also be overwritten before its replacement is secured.
findings.fix: When `prior.encrypted` is true, write the updated config directly as an encrypted envelope without first calling `saveConfig`.

findings.title: Broker account passwords are echoed at the prompt
findings.what: The account password is read with `ask()`, which uses the normal echoing readline prompt; the hidden-input `askSecret()` helper is not used.
findings.trigger: In a terminal setup, choose to configure a broker account and type its password.
findings.impact: The password is visible on screen and may be captured by terminal recording or scrollback.

findings.title: Confirmation links with tokens are returned unredacted
findings.what: The processed result includes the raw confirmation URL even though the module already has `redactedUrl()`. The caller prints this URL, exposing query tokens in stdout and any captured dashboard or service logs.
findings.trigger: Process a confirmation email whose link carries a token in its query string.
findings.impact: A bearer confirmation link, and potentially an embedded user identifier, is copied into logs where it can be replayed or disclosed.
findings.fix: Return a redacted URL in result objects and keep the raw URL only for navigation.

findings.title: Broker response snippets can persist the user's PII
findings.what: `judgeNewText()` returns raw text around confirmation wording as `detail`; the run loop logs that detail and passes it to state-recording functions. A broker page that echoes the submitted email or other identity data can therefore persist it in logs and state.
findings.trigger: A broker's success or email-confirmation page includes the user's email or name near its confirmation text.
findings.impact: PII is retained in run logs and `state.json`, where dashboard readers can also retrieve it.
findings.fix: Redact configured identity values from response snippets before logging or recording them, or store a fixed status detail instead.
